translation: Let me now explain the rules of chess.

We will now explain the winning and losing
conditions of chess.
There are two winning conditions in chess.

The first is to "checkmate” the opponent's
king.

Alternatively, the opponent might concede
the victory.

The inverse also applies for the losing
conditions.
The first is being checkmated.

Alternatively, you can concede the victory
yourself.

A "checkmate” happens when the king is in
"check”…

(The king is within movement range of the
opponent's pieces. The same as in shogi.)
…and has no way of getting out of check.
It is also possible to draw in chess.

There are four potential conditions for a
draw.
1. Reaching a "stalemate.”

2. The repetition of the same board state
three times.

3. If no pawn moves, or no pieces are taken
for 50 moves.
4. Agreeing to draw.

The fourth case often happens when the
players run out of pieces to checkmate with…

…or if the players decide that the match
won't come to a conclusion.

A "stalemate” occurs under the following
conditions.
The opponent's king is not in check.
The opponent has no pieces that can move.

When the above conditions are met, it is
judged as a "stalemate”…
…and the game ends in a draw.

There is an example of a "stalemate” in the
bottom screen.
Black has no pieces that can move.
The queen is covering all of the king's moves.
Also, their pawn is blocked by the white pawn.
However, black's king is not in "check.”

This state is considered a "stalemate” and
results in a draw.
I changed the state of the board slightly.
In this state, the black pawn can move.
In this case, there is no "stalemate”…
…and black must advance their pawn.
That's "checkmate.”

In this way, even if you have no chance of
winning…

…you can still draw by bringing it to a
"stalemate.”

Even if you can sense a victory, you have to
stay focused as you corner your opponent.

That concludes the explanation of the
winning and losing conditions.
